name: Warfarin and apixaban: medicines and food
headline: Taking warfarin or apixaban: why other medicines and food matter
summary: Bleeding is the main risk of both, so the NHS says other medicines, alcohol and, for warfarin, some foods and INR blood tests all matter.
keyPoints: Warfarin and apixaban are anticoagulants, medicines used to prevent and treat harmful blood clots.
The NHS says the amount of vitamin K-rich food should stay consistent on warfarin, and that cranberry products and grapefruit juice are avoided.
Warfarin needs regular INR blood tests, which measure how quickly the blood clots; apixaban does not need routine INR tests.
Both medicines can cause bleeding, and the NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding or after a head injury.
Anyone taking either medicine should check with a pharmacist before using other medicines, herbal products or supplements.

body.heading: What are warfarin and apixaban for?
body.body: Warfarin and apixaban are anticoagulant medicines, which are used to prevent and treat harmful blood clots. Warfarin belongs to a group that blocks vitamin K, which the liver needs to make clotting factors, so the blood takes longer to clot. Apixaban belongs to a different group called direct oral anticoagulants, or DOACs, which act on a very specific part of the clotting system. In atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm, the risk of stroke is higher, and anticoagulants are used to protect against clots. Both medicines make bleeding the main thing to watch for, which is why other medicines and some food and drink matter.

body.heading: Does food or drink matter with warfarin?
body.body: The NHS says some food and drink can change how warfarin works. Leafy green vegetables, chickpeas and liver contain a lot of vitamin K, which can interfere with warfarin. These foods do not have to be avoided, but the NHS says the amount eaten should stay consistent, because the clinic adjusts the dose to the person's usual diet. The NHS also says cranberry juice and cranberry products, and grapefruit juice, should be avoided, and that large amounts of alcohol should not be drunk. Warfarin can be taken with or without food.

body.heading: Does food or alcohol matter with apixaban?
body.body: NHS hospital leaflets describe no known interactions between apixaban and specific foods. They add that heavy drinking, especially binge drinking, can increase the effect of apixaban and make bleeding more likely.

body.heading: Which other medicines can interact?
body.body: The NHS says to tell a doctor, anticoagulant clinic or pharmacist before starting any new medicine on warfarin, including products bought over the counter. It also says St John's wort, a herbal remedy, and vitamin K supplements should not be taken with warfarin. For apixaban, the NHS lists other anticoagulants, some antifungal medicines, some heart and epilepsy medicines and SSRI antidepressants among those that can interact. The NHS says St John's wort should not be taken with apixaban, and that there is not enough evidence about other herbal remedies and supplements, so a pharmacist should be asked first. On painkillers, NHS advice says aspirin and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are generally avoided with anticoagulants unless a prescriber says otherwise. For everyday pain, the NHS lists paracetamol as the usual choice, though one NHS leaflet says long-term use can affect INR control on warfarin. A pharmacist can say whether a particular medicine, food product or supplement is suitable before it is bought.

body.heading: Why does warfarin need INR blood tests?
body.body: The NHS says warfarin treatment needs regular blood tests to measure how quickly the blood clots, called the international normalised ratio, or INR. Tests are more frequent at the start of treatment while the right dose is found, and become less frequent once the dose is stable. The clinic uses the result to adjust the warfarin dose, and the aim depends on the condition being treated. NHS booklets say apixaban and other DOACs do not need routine INR tests, although kidney function is checked before starting.

body.heading: What are the signs of bleeding, and who should be contacted?
body.body: Bleeding is the main risk of both medicines. For warfarin, the NHS lists blood in the urine or stools, unexplained bruising or nosebleeds, and coughing up or vomiting blood as signs to report. A sudden bad headache with confusion, slurred speech or difficulty moving the arms or legs can mean bleeding in the brain. For apixaban, the NHS describes bleeding more easily than usual, such as nosebleeds, bleeding gums, heavier periods, and bruises that fade slowly. The NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding, after a head injury, or for other serious side effects. NHS hospital leaflets say to call 999 or go to A&E for bleeding that will not stop, for signs of bleeding in the brain, or for swelling of the lips or throat with trouble breathing. The same leaflets say sudden breathlessness or chest pain can be a sign of a clot in the lung, which also needs 999. For questions that are not urgent, a GP, pharmacist or anticoagulant clinic can advise.

body.heading: What if a dose is missed?
body.body: The NHS pages for warfarin and apixaban each have their own advice on a forgotten dose. The sources note that the timing rules differ between the two medicines and between local services, so no single rule is given here. They agree that a missed dose should not be made up by taking two doses together. For warfarin, the NHS says the anticoagulant clinic should be contacted if doses are often missed. A pharmacist or GP can advise on a missed dose, NHS 111 gives urgent advice such as after taking too much, and 999 is for emergencies.
